opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship is actually much tighter than most people assume. There's a common view that you first build a really smart model, and then product people come along and wrap it into something useful. I don't think it works that way anymore.

From my experience working on reinforcement learning and agents, the intelligence you get is shaped by the environment you train in, and the product is, in a sense, the environment. When you put a model into a real product, users give you tasks you would never have designed in a lab. They expose failure modes, they define what "good" actually means. That feedback is the most valuable signal you can have for improving the model. So the product isn't just a consumer of intelligence; it's a source of it.

At the same time, I'd caution against the opposite extreme, where you over-engineer the product around the current model's weaknesses. Models improve very fast. If you build a lot of scaffolding, hand-written workflows, special rules, to patch today's limitations, six months later the base capability catches up and all that engineering becomes a burden. So the art is to design products that grow with the model: leave room for the model to do more over time, and make sure the data and interaction patterns from the product can flow back into training.

In RL terms, I'd say the product defines the reward and the task distribution, and the model provides the policy. You need both co-evolving. A team that only does models risks optimizing for benchmarks nobody cares about, and a team that only does products risks being commoditized by the next model release. The interesting place to be is where the two form a loop, where better models enable better products, and better products generate the data and signals to train better models. That flywheel, to me, is the core of building in AI right now.

r001.rationale: The response says products should grow with models and feed data back into training, but it does not frame product development as making the best use of the intelligence currently available.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention users avoiding questions because they expect the model to answer incorrectly.

r003.rationale: It notes that models improve quickly and advises leaving room for them to do more, but describes models and products as co-evolving rather than saying intelligence advances should run somewhat ahead of product development.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that for a long time these two things were pulled apart, and now they're being forced back together.

In the earlier wave of AI companies, you had a very clear division: the research team pushes the frontier of model capability, and the product team figures out how to package whatever comes out. Intelligence first, product second. That made sense when the models were so limited that the bottleneck was purely capability. Nobody cared about your UI if the model couldn't hold a coherent conversation.

But I think that framing is now wrong, or at least incomplete. Once models reach a certain level, the question stops being "how smart is it" and becomes "smart at what, for whom, in what context." And that's a product question. Which data do you collect, what feedback loop do you build, what does the user actually do with the output, where does the human stay in the loop. Those decisions shape the intelligence itself, because the model learns from the environment the product creates.

So my view is that intelligence and product shouldn't be in a pipeline, one feeding the other. They should be a loop. The product defines the real-world task and generates the signal; the model improves against that signal; the improved model unlocks a product you couldn't build before. If you're an AI company and your research and product teams don't talk to each other every week, you're going to lose to someone whose teams do.

There's also a trap on the other side, which is being product-only. You can wrap an API in a nice interface and get early traction, but if you don't have some proprietary understanding of the model, the data, or the task, you have no moat. The platform underneath you moves and your product moves with it, whether you like it or not.

So I'd put it like this: intelligence without product is a demo, product without intelligence is a wrapper. The companies that matter will be the ones that treat them as one problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says product choices help shape intelligence and advocates a feedback loop between product and models; it does not frame product development as making the best use of intelligence already available.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses user tasks and feedback, but does not mention users withholding questions because they expect the model to answer incorrectly.

r003.rationale: The candidate rejects a pipeline in which intelligence comes first and product second, and instead argues for a loop. It does not say intelligence advances should run somewhat ahead of product development.

astra-6.text:
I think intelligence and product development need to evolve together. A stronger model creates new possibilities, but a good product helps us understand which capabilities actually matter to people.

For example, a model might give a very impressive answer in a demo. But when you build a product around it, you discover that users need it to understand their context, handle mistakes, and complete a task reliably. Those requirements should feed back into how you develop the AI.

So I wouldn’t treat it as a sequence where we first solve intelligence and then figure out the product. You need a continuous loop: improve the model, put it into a useful workflow, learn where it fails, and use that experience to guide the next improvement. The measure of progress is whether people can accomplish something they couldn’t accomplish before.

r001.rationale: The response says product development helps reveal which AI capabilities matter and improve workflows, but does not frame it as making the best use of the intelligence currently available.

r002.rationale: It mentions users needing context and reliability, but does not say they may avoid asking questions because they expect the model to answer incorrectly.

r003.rationale: The response advocates a continuous feedback loop and says intelligence and product development should evolve together; it does not say AI advances should run somewhat ahead.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they need to evolve together. Intelligence creates new possibilities for products, while building products reveals what intelligence is actually useful—and where it still falls short.

A model might perform very well on a benchmark, but a user cares about whether it can solve a particular problem reliably. Can it understand what they mean? Can it finish the task? How much supervision does it need? Those questions should influence both the product design and the development of the AI.

At the same time, we shouldn’t simply put AI into an existing interface and assume that’s the product. If the capabilities change, we should reconsider the workflow itself: what the user needs to do, what the AI can take on, and where the user should remain in control.

So I see it as a continuous feedback loop. Build around the capabilities you have, learn from real use, and let that learning guide the next improvements in intelligence.

r001.rationale: It says to build around the AI capabilities currently available and learn from real use, communicating that product development should make use of current intelligence.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability and understanding user needs, but does not say users may avoid asking questions because they expect the model to answer incorrectly.

r003.rationale: It describes intelligence and product development as evolving together in a feedback loop; it does not argue that advances in intelligence should run ahead of product development.
